strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to incorporate heavy masking into supervised training. Shared parameters and detached predictions from the unmasked branch avoid an additional teacher or inference overhead, while token removal reduces the masked branch's training cost.

The main ImageNet results provide convincing evidence of practical value. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across four ViT sizes at 400 epochs. Table A.13 supports the repeatability of the main result: ViT-B achieves 84.08 ± 0.02 versus the reported baseline's 83.46 ± 0.04 over three runs.

The paper meaningfully addresses the additional computation. In Table 8, ViT-B with MaskSub reaches 84.1% using 25 GPU days, compared with 83.7% using 26 GPU days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy/cost tradeoff against CoSub. These controls strengthen the contribution beyond comparisons at equal epochs.

Evaluation spans several strong training recipes, architectures, and downstream tasks. Evidence includes MAE/BEiTv2/CLIP finetuning, ResNet and Swin training, ADE20K segmentation, and COCO detection. Robustness improvements are substantial in some settings: Table A.4 reports ImageNet-A accuracy increasing from 51.9% to 58.3% for ViT-H.

Algorithm 1 and Appendix B make the core implementation reasonably reproducible. Masking-ratio and loss-weight ablations, repeated trials for selected experiments, and a supplied code link provide useful supporting documentation. The supported empirical contribution makes the case for weak acceptance stronger than the reservations below.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is narrower than the framing suggests. With a detached teacher distribution, Equation (3)'s cross-entropy has the same student gradient as KL consistency regularization. Consequently, Section 2's distinction between MaskSub's 'distillation loss' and UDA's 'consistency loss' does not establish a fundamentally different objective. The originality primarily concerns efficient masking and its effective integration into supervised recipes.

The proposed explanation of 'automatic difficulty control' exceeds the evidence. Figure 2 shows aggregate gradient magnitudes and improved convergence, but does not establish the claim that masking effectively applies exclusively to successfully predicted examples. Equation (3) contains no correctness gate, and a confidently incorrect prediction can still provide a strong target. The optimization benefit is supported more directly than this sample-wise interpretation.

The method is not uniformly beneficial as a finetuning plug-in. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 also acknowledges that CLIP's best-checkpoint accuracy is unchanged despite improved final-epoch accuracy. These findings materially qualify claims of improvements across all cases.

Some secondary comparisons are less conclusive than the main ViT evidence. Several Table 6 comparisons combine different training recipes, although the RSB-matched comparisons are useful. Small gains such as BEiTv2's 0.1 percentage point improvements lack reported run variability, leaving their reliability less established.

The central KD ablation has a correctable reporting ambiguity. Table A.6 identifies a 'w/o KD loss' condition without explicitly defining whether the masked branch instead receives ground-truth supervision or no loss. This limits its ability to isolate the benefit of soft targets from the choice of which views receive supervision.
